tagline: Building a future that is more human
note: Lessons summarize and apply ideas in our own words. Items with origin 'By Design' are our application, not the author's. 'verify' lists open checks before publishing.

books.title: Tiny Habits
books.subtitle: The Small Changes That Change Everything
books.author: BJ Fogg, PhD
books.pitch: The founder of Stanford's Behavior Design Lab explains why big changes rarely stick, and how starting absurdly small, in the right spot in your day, makes new habits grow on their own. [1,2]
whyRead: A simple model that explains why any behavior does or doesn't happen [3]
A step-by-step method you can use on any habit, at home or at work [1,6]
Dozens of real stories from people who used it, with recipes you can copy [1]

bigIdea.name: Start tiny, and make it feel good
bigIdea.body: Fogg argues that relying on motivation is a trap, because it rises and falls like a wave. Shrink a new habit until it's easy on your worst day, attach it to something you already do, and celebrate the moment you do it. The good feeling is what wires the habit in. [1,4,5]

learnings.title: Motivation is unreliable
learnings.text: Use a high-motivation moment for one-off actions, like signing up or setting things up. For daily habits, rely on ease instead. [4]

learnings.title: Emotions create habits
learnings.text: Fogg's term for the feeling of success right after a behavior is Shine. A quick, genuine celebration does more to build a habit than repetition alone. [5]

learnings.title: Help yourself feel successful
learnings.text: Choose behaviors you actually want to do and can do, rather than ones you feel you should. Small wins build the confidence for bigger ones. [1,6]

framework.name: The Fogg Behavior Model
framework.intro: A Behavior happens when Motivation, Ability and a Prompt come together at the same moment. If a behavior isn't happening, one of the three is missing. [3]

parts.name: Motivation
parts.text: Real, but it rises and falls through the day in what Fogg calls the Motivation Wave. [4]
parts.tip: Match yourself with behaviors you already want. [1]

parts.name: Ability
parts.text: Fogg's Ability Chain: time, money, physical effort, mental effort and fit with your routine. The weakest link decides how hard it feels. [6]
parts.tip: Make it tiny: a Starter Step, or a scaled-back version. [6]

parts.name: Prompt
parts.tagline: What tells you to do it now
parts.text: Three kinds: Person prompts (a feeling), Context prompts (something around you) and Action prompts (a routine you already do). [7]
parts.tip: Use an Action prompt, which Fogg calls an Anchor. [7]

tools.name: The ABC recipe
tools.note: Fogg's formula for a new habit: Anchor, Behavior, Celebration. [8,11]
steps: Pick an Anchor: a routine you never skip, like starting the coffee machine.
Choose a tiny Behavior that takes under 30 seconds.
Write it as: After I [anchor], I will [behavior].
Celebrate right away, in a way that feels real to you.

tools.name: Swarm and Focus Map
tools.note: Fogg's way to pick the right behaviors for a goal. [6,10]
steps: Write the outcome you want at the centre of a page.
Swarm it: list every specific behavior that could help.
Plot each one by impact and by how likely you are to do it.
Start with the Golden Behaviors: high on both.
Write one Tiny Habits recipe using the ABC formula.
Try Fogg's Maui Habit: each morning, as your feet touch the floor, tell yourself it's going to be a great day. [9]
Turn an annoyance into a cue, which Fogg calls a Pearl Habit. [6]
After seven days, notice which recipe stuck, and scale it up a little.

reflect: Which habit have you been trying to start with willpower alone?
What's the smallest version of it you'd do even on your worst day?
books.inSedi: Save your recipe as a Routine in Timely. The little sound when you tick it is a ready-made celebration.

sources.text: Fogg, BJ. *Tiny Habits: The Small Changes That Change Everything*. Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2019 (© 2020).

books.title: Indistractable
books.subtitle: How to Control Your Attention and Choose Your Life
books.author: Nir Eyal with Julie Li
books.pitch: Nir Eyal, who once wrote about building habit-forming products, turns to the other side: how to stop distraction from running your day, with a four-part model and dozens of practical tactics. [1,2,3,7]
whyRead: A fresh take: distraction starts inside us, not in our phones [3]
Tactics for email, meetings, group chat and your phone [3,4]
Chapters on raising indistractable kids and building focused workplaces [4]

bigIdea.name: Distraction is an escape from discomfort
bigIdea.body: Eyal argues that most distraction is an attempt to escape an uncomfortable feeling such as boredom, loneliness or worry. Technology is only the proximate cause. Learn to handle the feeling, plan your time around your values, and the pull of distraction loses much of its power. [3,4]

learnings.title: Traction vs. distraction
learnings.text: Traction is any action that moves you toward what you intend; distraction moves you away. You can only call something a distraction if you know what you meant to do. [3]

learnings.title: Ask of every trigger
learnings.text: Is this trigger serving me, or am I serving it? Keep the pings that lead to traction and remove the rest. [3,6]

learnings.title: Willpower isn't a battery
learnings.text: Eyal reviews research suggesting that believing willpower runs out makes us give up sooner. Reimagine your temperament as well as the task. [4]

framework.name: The Indistractable Model
framework.intro: Eyal's four-part model, from the inside out. [3]

parts.name: Master internal triggers
parts.text: Notice the feeling that comes before distraction, and stay with it instead of escaping. [3]
parts.tip: The 10-minute rule: wait ten minutes before giving in. [3,5]

parts.name: Make time for traction
parts.text: Timebox your week across three domains: You, Relationships and Work. [3]
parts.tip: Schedule sync: agree your calendar with those who depend on it. [4,6]

parts.name: Hack back external triggers
parts.text: Tactics for email, group chat, meetings, your phone and your desktop. [3,4]
parts.tip: No agenda, no meeting. [6]

parts.name: Prevent distraction with pacts
parts.text: Effort pacts add friction, price pacts put money at stake, and identity pacts change how you see yourself. [3]
parts.tip: Call yourself indistractable, and act like it. [3]

tools.name: The Distraction Tracker
tools.note: Eyal's log for finding your internal triggers. [3]
steps: Keep a card or note open while you work.
Each time you get distracted, write the time and the feeling just before.
After three days, look for the most common feelings and triggers.
Choose one fix for the biggest one.

tools.name: The timeboxed week
tools.note: Eyal's way to turn values into a calendar. [3]
steps: Start from a blank weekly template.
Add blocks for You, then Relationships, then Work.
Follow it for a week, then reflect and refine.
Share it with your manager or partner.
Run the Distraction Tracker for three days.
Try the 10-minute rule on the most common urge.
Turn off every notification that doesn't come from a person.
Timebox next week across You, Relationships and Work.

reflect: What feeling usually comes right before you get distracted?
Which trigger around you serves someone else's goals, not yours?
books.inSedi: Timebox your week in Timely's day view, including blocks for yourself and your people, not just work.

sources.text: Eyal, Nir, with Julie Li. *Indistractable: How to Control Your Attention and Choose Your Life*. BenBella Books, 2019. Part 1 internal triggers (ch. 6 the 10-minute rule); Part 2 traction (ch. 12 schedule sync); Part 3 external triggers (ch. 17 meetings); Part 4 pacts (ch. 23–25).

books.title: Atomic Habits
books.subtitle: An Easy & Proven Way to Build Good Habits & Break Bad Ones
books.author: James Clear
books.pitch: James Clear shows how tiny improvements compound into remarkable results, and gives a practical system for designing the cues, cravings and rewards behind every habit you want to build or break. [1,2,9]
whyRead: A clear, memorable system you can apply to any habit [2]
Stories from athletes, artists and scientists that make the ideas stick [1]
Practical tools like habit stacking and the Two-Minute Rule [6,8]

bigIdea.name: Systems beat goals
bigIdea.body: Clear argues that goals set the direction but systems make the progress: you fall to the level of your systems. Getting about 1% better each day compounds, even when results stay invisible for a long time. He calls that stretch the Plateau of Latent Potential. [1,2,3]

learnings.title: Every action is a vote
learnings.text: Habits shape identity. Decide who you want to become, then prove it to yourself with small wins. Change works best from identity outward. [4]

learnings.title: Environment beats willpower
learnings.text: Make the cues for good habits obvious and hide the cues for bad ones. The easiest habit is the one already set up for you. [2]

learnings.title: Never miss twice
learnings.text: Missing once is an accident. Missing twice is the start of a new pattern, so get straight back on track. [10]

framework.name: The Four Laws of Behavior Change
framework.intro: Every habit runs through a loop: cue, craving, response, reward. Each law shapes one stage. To break a habit, invert the law. [2]

parts.name: Make it obvious
parts.text: A habit starts with a cue you notice. Decide exactly when and where you'll act. [2,6]
parts.tip: I will [behavior] at [time] in [location]. [6]

parts.name: Make it attractive
parts.text: The more appealing a habit, the more likely you'll do it. [2]
parts.tip: Temptation bundling: pair a need with a want. [7]

parts.name: Make it easy
parts.text: Reduce friction for good habits and add it to bad ones. [2]
parts.tip: Two-Minute Rule: start with a version under two minutes. [8]

parts.name: Make it satisfying
parts.text: We repeat what feels good straight away. [2]
parts.tip: Track it so progress is visible. [10]

tools.name: The Habits Scorecard
tools.note: Clear's exercise for noticing what you already do. [5]
steps: List everything you do from the moment you wake up.
Mark each habit +, – or = for the person you want to be.
Don't change anything yet. Just notice.

tools.name: Habit stacking
tools.note: Clear's formula for linking a new habit to an old one. [6]
steps: List habits you already do every day without fail.
Pick one that happens at the right time and place.
Write it: After [current habit], I will [new habit].
Make the cue precise, like “when I close my laptop at lunch”.
Do the Habits Scorecard for one ordinary day.
Pick one new habit and shrink it to two minutes.
Stack it onto an existing habit.
Track it every day, and never miss twice.

reflect: Which of your current habits are votes for the person you want to become?
What does your current system reliably produce?
books.inSedi: Add the stacked habit as a daily Routine in Timely and tick it off to keep your streak visible.

sources.text: Clear, James. *Atomic Habits*. Avery, 2018. Ch. 1–2 (1% gains, Plateau of Latent Potential, identity), ch. 4 (Habits Scorecard), ch. 5 (implementation intentions, habit stacking), ch. 8 (temptation bundling), ch. 13 (Two-Minute Rule), ch. 16 (habit tracking, never miss twice).
Clear, James. “Atomic Habits: summary”, jamesclear.com.

Clear, James. “Habit Stacking”, jamesclear.com.

books.title: Nudge
books.subtitle: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness
books.author: Richard H. Thaler and Cass R. Sunstein
books.publisher: Yale University Press; updated as *Nudge: The Final Edition* (Penguin, 2021)
books.pitch: A Nobel-winning economist and a legal scholar show how small changes in the way choices are presented can help people make better decisions about their health, money and happiness, without taking any options away. [1,2,3]
whyRead: The book that brought behavioral economics into everyday policy and design [2]
Memorable real examples, from cafeterias to pension plans [2,4]
The Final Edition adds sludge, climate and the pandemic [5,6]

bigIdea.name: There is no neutral design
bigIdea.body: Someone always decides how options are arranged: what comes first, what's the default, what takes effort. Thaler and Sunstein call that person a choice architect. Since design always influences choice, they argue for designing on purpose to help people while keeping every option open, which they call libertarian paternalism. [2,4]

learnings.title: Humans, not Econs
learnings.text: Economic models assume perfectly rational Econs. Real Humans think with a fast Automatic System and a slow Reflective System, and make predictable mistakes. [2,7]

learnings.title: Defaults are powerful
learnings.text: Many people stick with whatever happens if they do nothing. Automatic enrolment in retirement savings is the book's classic example. [2,8]

learnings.title: Beware of sludge
learnings.text: The Final Edition adds the opposite of a nudge: friction that makes good choices harder, like long forms and hard-to-cancel subscriptions. [5,6]

framework.name: NUDGES
framework.intro: The authors' checklist of choice-architecture tools. Each letter is one lever. [9]

parts.name: iNcentives
parts.text: People respond to incentives they actually notice. [9]
parts.tip: Show the real cost at the moment of choice.

parts.name: Understand mappings
parts.text: Help people see what each option means for things they care about. [9]
parts.tip: Translate features into results.

parts.name: Defaults
parts.tagline: What happens if you do nothing
parts.text: Set the default to what most people would choose on reflection. [2,9]
parts.tip: Make the good option automatic.

parts.name: Give feedback · Expect error
parts.text: Tell people how they're doing, and design so common mistakes are hard to make, like a cash machine that returns your card first. [9]
parts.tip: Add a forcing function for the usual slip.

parts.name: Structure complex choices
parts.text: As choices grow, help people narrow them down. [9]
parts.tip: Offer filters for what matters most.

tools.name: Save More Tomorrow
tools.note: A program by Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi, described in the book. [2,10]
steps: Commit now to save more in the future.
Tie each increase to your next pay rise.
Let it happen automatically, and stay free to opt out.

tools.name: A sludge audit
tools.note: Applying the Final Edition's sludge chapter to your own life. [5,6]
steps: Pick a good habit you keep skipping.
Time each step it takes.
Remove or prefill one step.
Add one step of friction to a habit you want less of.
List five recurring choices: savings, subscriptions, your phone's home screen, snacks, calendar invites.
For each, write what happens if you do nothing.
Change two defaults to what you'd choose on reflection.
Run a sludge audit on one good habit.

reflect: Where are you living with a default you never chose?
Whose choices do you shape, at home or at work?
books.inSedi: Make good choices the default in Sedi too: set up a daily Routine in Timely, and use the trash for anything you never act on.

books.title: Feel-Good Productivity
books.subtitle: How to Do More of What Matters to You
books.author: Ali Abdaal
books.pitch: A doctor-turned-YouTuber makes the case that feeling good is the engine of productivity, not the reward for it, and gives research-backed experiments for bringing more energy into your work. [1,2]
whyRead: A warm, practical book that makes productivity feel lighter [2]
Every chapter ends with small experiments to try [2]
Clear explanations of the research behind each idea [1,3]

bigIdea.name: Feeling good comes first
bigIdea.body: Abdaal argues the discipline-and-pressure approach has it backwards. Positive feelings give us energy, energy makes work easier to start and keep going, and progress then feels good too. So instead of forcing yourself to work, change how the work feels. [1,2,3]

learnings.title: Make it fun
learnings.text: Ask: what would this look like if it were fun? Small changes, like music, a game, or doing it with someone, can transform a dull task. [3]

learnings.title: Goals that energise
learnings.text: Abdaal suggests NICE goals: Near-term, Input-based, Controllable and Energising, instead of distant targets you can't control. [2,4]

learnings.title: Three kinds of burnout
learnings.text: Overexertion (doing too much), depletion (not recharging) and misalignment (doing what doesn't fit you). Each needs a different fix. [2,3]

framework.name: Energise · Unblock · Sustain
framework.intro: The book's three parts: what gives us energy, what stops us starting, and what keeps us going. [1,2]

parts.name: Energise
parts.text: Lightness and curiosity, a sense of confidence and control, and feeling part of something with others. [2,3]
parts.tip: Teach what you're learning to build confidence. [12]

parts.name: Unblock
parts.text: Seek clarity, find courage, and make starting easy. [2]
parts.tip: Commit to just five minutes. [6]

parts.name: Sustain
parts.text: Protect your energy, refill it, and make sure your work points where you want to go. [2,3]
parts.tip: Sketch alternative futures with an Odyssey Plan. [5,9]

tools.name: Taming fear
tools.note: Fear tools from the Unblock chapters, each borrowed and credited by Abdaal. [7]
steps: Name the feeling in a word.
Ask how much it will matter in 10 minutes, 10 months and 10 years (Suzy Welch's 10/10/10). [8]
Remember the spotlight effect: others notice us far less than we think. [10]

tools.name: The Energy Investment Portfolio
tools.note: Abdaal's way to avoid overexertion. [5,11]
steps: List every commitment and dream competing for your energy.
Choose about five active investments.
Move the rest to a someday list.
Review the portfolio each season.
Pick the task you've been avoiding most.
Change one thing to make it more fun.
Rewrite the goal as a NICE goal.
Set a five-minute timer and start.

reflect: Which blocker shows up most for you: uncertainty, fear or inertia?
Which kind of burnout are you closest to?
books.inSedi: Write the NICE goal on the task in Taskly and move it to In progress.

sources.text: Abdaal, Ali. *Feel-Good Productivity: How to Do More of What Matters to You*. Celadon Books, 2023. Part 1 Energise (ch. 1–3), Part 2 Unblock (ch. 4–6), Part 3 Sustain (ch. 7–9).

books.title: The Fun Habit
books.subtitle: How the Pursuit of Joy and Wonder Can Change Your Life
books.author: Mike Rucker, PhD
books.pitch: A behavioral scientist argues that fun isn't frivolous. It's a skill you can plan and practice, and making room for it can change how you feel about your whole life. [1,2]
whyRead: A playful, research-backed case for taking fun seriously [2,3]
Simple tools for finding fun in ordinary days [3]
A warm reminder that life is short, so enjoy it on purpose [2]

bigIdea.name: Do fun, don't chase happiness
bigIdea.body: Rucker separates chasing happiness as a feeling, which often backfires, from doing fun things, which you can actually choose. He also points to research suggesting that feeling good now makes it easier to choose harder, longer-term activities later. [2,3,4]

learnings.title: Audit your time
learnings.text: Most of us don't know where our hours go. Rucker recommends a time audit to find room for fun that's already there. [5]

learnings.title: Keep a Fun File
learnings.text: A ready list of 8 to 15 go-to fun options, so free time doesn't default to scrolling. [2,5]

learnings.title: Fun is a choice
learnings.text: Fun rarely happens after the work is done. It happens when you plan for it like anything else that matters. [2,3]

framework.name: The PLAY Model
framework.intro: Sort your activities on two axes: challenge (what they cost you) and fun (how much you enjoy them). [6]

parts.name: Pleasing
parts.text: Easy and enjoyable. Rucker treats these as the everyday goal. [6]
parts.tip: Build them into your routine.

parts.name: Living
parts.text: Peak experiences that take effort or risk. Not daily, but worth real space in your life. [6]
parts.tip: Plan a few each year.

parts.name: Agonizing
parts.text: Costly and unpleasant. Some, like taxes, can't be avoided. [6]
parts.tip: Eliminate what you can.

parts.name: Yielding
parts.text: Easy but empty habits that quietly eat time. [6]
parts.tip: Swap them for something Pleasing.

tools.name: SAVOR
tools.note: Rucker's five tools for more fun in ordinary days. [3,7]
steps: Story editing: retell the story you tell about your time (an idea from Timothy Wilson). [8]
Activity bundling: pair a must-do with a want-to. [9]
Variable hedonics and Options: add variety and keep fun choices ready.
Reminiscing: revisit good memories on purpose.

tools.name: Time audit and PLAY sort
tools.note: Combining two of the book's tools. [5,6]
steps: Log yesterday hour by hour.
Place each activity in a PLAY quadrant.
Find one Yielding activity to swap for something from your Fun File.
Do a time audit for one day.
Sort it with the PLAY model.
Start a Fun File and trim it to 8 to 15 options.
Put one Pleasing activity on the calendar.

reflect: Which quadrant does most of your free time fall into?
What reliably makes you lose track of time in a good way?
books.inSedi: Keep your Fun File as a note in Brainly, and put one Pleasing activity on this week's calendar in Timely.

books.title: The Organized Mind
books.subtitle: Thinking Straight in the Age of Information Overload
books.author: Daniel J. Levitin
books.pitch: A neuroscientist explains how attention and memory actually work, then shows how to organize your home, your time and your decisions around their limits. [1,2]
whyRead: A clear tour of how your attention system works [3,4]
Practical advice for homes, time, work and big decisions [1,5]
A brilliant appendix on thinking clearly about risk [1,5]

bigIdea.name: Get it out of your head
bigIdea.body: Conscious attention can only handle a small amount of information at a time; Levitin estimates around 120 bits per second. Every open loop you hold in your head competes for that space. Moving information into the world, into places and systems you trust, frees your mind to think. [1,6]

learnings.title: Multitasking is switching
learnings.text: We don't really do two things at once. We switch rapidly, and every switch costs energy and adds errors. [6,7]

learnings.title: Give things a home
learnings.text: Designated places for things you often lose, like a hook for your keys, let the environment do the remembering. [5]

learnings.title: Good enough is often best
learnings.text: For small decisions, satisfice: accept good enough and save your effort for the choices that matter. The idea comes from Herbert Simon. [7,8]

framework.name: How attention works
framework.intro: Levitin describes several parts of the attentional system. Knowing them explains why focus slips. [3,5]

parts.name: Mind-wandering mode
parts.text: A loose, associative state where ideas connect and the brain rests. [3]
parts.tip: Protect time with no input at all.

parts.name: Central executive
parts.text: The mode for deliberate work. It and mind-wandering tend to switch each other off. [3,5]
parts.tip: Give it one thing at a time.

parts.name: Attentional filter
parts.text: Screens the flood of input so only some reaches awareness. [3,5]
parts.tip: Cut low-value inputs at the source.

parts.name: Attentional switch
parts.text: Shifts you between focus and wandering. Each switch has a cost. [3,6]
parts.tip: Batch similar tasks together.

tools.name: Index-card capture
tools.note: Levitin's low-tech system for open loops. [3,5]
steps: Write each task or idea on its own card.
Sort the cards each day: do now, and later.
Re-sort as priorities change.

tools.name: The fourfold table
tools.note: From the book's appendix, for reasoning about risk. [1,5]
steps: Draw a 2 by 2 grid: test result against actual condition.
Fill it with counts per 1,000 people.
Read off the real chance that a positive result means you have the condition.
Spend five minutes writing every open loop, one per card or note.
Sort them into now and later.
Give one thing you often lose a fixed home.
Batch your replies into one block a day.

reflect: What are you holding in your head that could live somewhere else?
Where in your day do you switch most often?
books.inSedi: Brain-dump onto the Universal Board, one card per thought, then drag each to Taskly, Timely or Brainly.

sources.text: Levitin, Daniel J. *The Organized Mind: Thinking Straight in the Age of Information Overload*. Dutton, 2014. books.title: The Leading Brain
books.subtitle: Powerful Science-Based Strategies for Achieving Peak Performance
books.author: Friederike Fabritius and Hans W. Hagemann
books.pitch: A neuropsychologist and a leadership consultant translate brain science into practical strategies for performing at your best, managing emotions, building habits and leading teams. [1,2,3]
whyRead: Brain science made practical for everyday work [2,4]
Concrete techniques for stress, focus and habits [4]
A fresh look at what makes teams work well together [3,4]

bigIdea.name: Find your sweet spot
bigIdea.body: You do your best work at a moderate level of arousal: too little and you're bored, too much and you panic. This curve goes back to Yerkes and Dodson in 1908. The authors show how to tune the task, the setting or the stakes so you stay in the zone where focus, and sometimes flow, come naturally. [3,4,5,10]

learnings.title: Name the feeling
learnings.text: Labelling an emotion helps restore control. Suppressing it competes with your thinking. [3,7,9]

learnings.title: Habits slip in small
learnings.text: A large share of daily behavior runs on habit. Small, low-threat steps help new habits form without resistance. [4,8]

learnings.title: Mix your team
learnings.text: Drawing on Helen Fisher's research, the authors describe four temperaments. Strong teams combine them. [4,11]

framework.name: Peak · Change · Teams
framework.intro: The book's three parts, each with three chapters. [6]

parts.name: Reach your peak
parts.text: Performance depends on a balance of brain chemicals the authors call a neurococktail. [2,12]
parts.tip: Use STOP: Stop, Take a breath, Observe, Proceed. [4]

parts.name: Change your brain
parts.text: Build habits in small steps, and give weight to intuition in complex decisions. [4,8]
parts.tip: Write down a goal that matters to you emotionally. [4]

parts.name: Build dream teams
parts.text: Explorer, Builder, Director and Negotiator temperaments, plus trust that keeps people in a reward state rather than a threat state. [3,4,11]
parts.tip: Social pain registers much like physical pain. [3,8]

tools.name: The sweet-spot audit
tools.note: Based on the book's approach to peak performance. [4]
steps: List your typical week's activities.
Tag each: bored, stressed, or top of your game.
Turn bored tasks up with challenge or a deadline.
Turn stressful tasks down by breaking them up or getting support.

tools.name: STOP
tools.note: A short reset the authors recommend. [4]
steps: Stop what you're doing.
Take a breath.
Observe your thoughts, feelings and body.
Proceed, on purpose.
Rate today's main task from 1 (bored) to 10 (overwhelmed).
Under 4, add a challenge. Over 7, break it into steps.
Use STOP before one stressful moment each day.
Each night, write three things you're grateful for, and protect your sleep.

reflect: When were you last at the top of your game, and what made it possible?
Which temperament is missing from your team?
books.inSedi: Break an overwhelming task into small steps as a project in Timely's Planning view.

books.title: The Brain That Changes Itself
books.subtitle: Stories of Personal Triumph from the Frontiers of Brain Science
books.author: Norman Doidge, MD
books.pitch: A psychiatrist tells the stories of the scientists and patients who showed that the adult brain keeps rewiring itself, overturning the old belief that it was fixed for life. [1,2,3]
whyRead: Gripping true stories of recovery and discovery [3,4]
An accessible introduction to neuroplasticity [3]
A hopeful, scientific case that change is possible at any age [4]

bigIdea.name: What you practise, you become
bigIdea.body: For a long time, scientists thought each brain region did one fixed job. Doidge tells the story of the research that showed otherwise: what we repeatedly do and pay attention to physically reshapes the brain. That cuts both ways, so choose what you rehearse. [1,3,4]

learnings.title: Use it or lose it
learnings.text: Brain territory is contested. Skills you practise claim more of it; skills you neglect lose ground. [4,5]

learnings.title: The plastic paradox
learnings.text: The flexibility that lets us change also locks in rigid habits. Doidge compares it to ski tracks: the more a path is used, the harder it is to leave. [6,7]

learnings.title: Attention is the key
learnings.text: Doidge reports Michael Merzenich's finding that lasting change in brain maps needs close attention. Divided attention doesn't produce it. [8]

framework.name: How the brain rewires
framework.intro: Four ideas that run through the book's case studies. [3,4]

parts.name: Fire together, wire together
parts.text: Neurons active at the same time strengthen their links. The phrase sums up Donald Hebb's rule. [10,12]
parts.tip: Pair a habit with a consistent cue and place.

parts.name: Competitive plasticity
parts.text: Practised skills expand; neglected ones shrink. [4,5]
parts.tip: Practise what you want to keep.

parts.name: Mental practice
parts.text: Alvaro Pascual-Leone found mental practice of piano changed brain maps much like physical practice. [8]
parts.tip: Rehearse vividly before you practise.

parts.name: Constraint
parts.text: Edward Taub's therapy restrains the strong limb so the weak one relearns, in small graded steps. [9]
parts.tip: Remove the shortcut you lean on.

tools.name: Mental rehearsal
tools.note: Inspired by Pascual-Leone's research in the book. [8]
steps: Pick one skill.
Rehearse it vividly in your head for five minutes.
Then practise it for real with full attention.
Track progress over a week.

tools.name: Interrupt and refocus
tools.note: From the book's chapter on obsessive loops. [5]
steps: When a worry loop or urge starts, name it as a habit circuit, not a fact.
Switch to a planned, rewarding activity for about 15 minutes.
Log it, and notice the loop weakening over time.
Pick one skill to grow.
Rehearse it in your head for five minutes a day.
Practise for ten minutes with full attention and one shortcut removed.
Keep it little and often: steady practice beats cramming. [11]

reflect: What have you been unintentionally practising lately?
Which skill are you losing because you stopped using it?
books.inSedi: Make the practice a daily Routine in Timely, and keep progress notes in Brainly.

sources.text: Doidge, Norman. *The Brain That Changes Itself*. Viking, 2007. Ch. 1 A Woman Perpetually Falling; ch. 3 Redesigning the Brain; ch. 5 Midnight Resurrections; ch. 6 Brain Lock Unlocked; ch. 8 Imagination.

books.title: The Blue Zones of Happiness
books.subtitle: Lessons from the World's Happiest People
books.author: Dan Buettner
books.pitch: The explorer behind the Blue Zones longevity research visits the happiest places on Earth and shows how to redesign your own surroundings so wellbeing becomes the easy default. Foreword by Ed Diener. [1,2]
whyRead: Vivid reporting from Costa Rica, Denmark and Singapore [1,3]
Practical changes for your home, work, friendships and money [4,6]
A self-test to find where your happiness is thin [1,4]

bigIdea.name: Shape your surroundings
bigIdea.body: Buettner's reporting suggests the happiest people don't try harder. They live in places that make good days easy: walkable streets, short commutes, close friends nearby, homes that invite rest. Change your environment, and your behavior follows. [1,4,5]

learnings.title: Social time matters
learnings.text: Buettner points to research suggesting the happiest people spend about six hours a day with others, far more than most people do. [6,8]

learnings.title: The commute is a tax
learnings.text: Long commutes drag down happiness. Living close enough to walk to work is ideal. [4,6]

learnings.title: Purpose beats pay
learnings.text: In Denmark, a strong safety net frees people to choose work for interest rather than need. [3,5]

framework.name: The Three Strands of Happiness
framework.intro: Buettner braids happiness from three strands, and finds a country that excels at each. [1,3]

parts.name: Pleasure
parts.text: Day-to-day positive emotion. Costa Ricans enjoy strong family and faith ties and lots of daily socializing. [3,4]
parts.tip: Build more small, shared rituals into each day.

parts.name: Purpose
parts.text: Meaningful activity that uses your strengths, supported by trust, clubs and volunteering. [3,4,5]
parts.tip: Join a club or volunteer. [6]

parts.name: Pride
parts.text: How you rate your life overall. Singapore scores high thanks to security and clear paths to success. [3,4]
parts.tip: Live within your means and set reachable goals. [7]

tools.name: The Happiness Test
tools.note: The book's self-test for finding your weakest strand. [1,4]
steps: Take the test, or rate pleasure, purpose and pride from 1 to 10.
Find your weakest strand.
Read the chapter for the area of life most tied to it.

tools.name: Design your Life Radius
tools.note: The book's practical chapters, one area of life at a time. [1,2]
steps: Community: favour walkability, nature and trust. [4]
Workplace and home: shorten the commute; keep the TV out of the main room. [4]
Social life: a few close friends, a weekly family meal. [6]
Inner life: know your purpose, volunteer, try new things. [9]
Rate pleasure, purpose and pride from 1 to 10.
Log how many hours you spent with people yesterday.
Make one change to your surroundings.
Start one standing social ritual.

reflect: Which strand is thinnest in your life right now?
What in your surroundings makes a good day harder than it needs to be?
books.inSedi: Give each strand its own board in Boardly, with one goal on each.

sources.text: Buettner, Dan. *The Blue Zones of Happiness*. National Geographic, 2017. Ch. 3–5 (Costa Rica, Denmark, Singapore); ch. 7–12 (Designing happy communities, workplace, social network, home, financial well-being, inner life).

books.title: Designing Your Work Life
books.subtitle: How to Thrive and Change and Find Happiness at Work
books.author: Bill Burnett and Dave Evans
books.pitch: The authors of *Designing Your Life* bring design thinking to the job you already have, so you can make it better before deciding whether to leave. Reissued in 2021 as *Designing Your New Work Life*. [1,2]
whyRead: Practical exercises for anyone who feels stuck at work [3,4]
A humane take on money, meaning, burnout and office politics [5]
Smart advice on how to quit well, if you do decide to go [6,8]

bigIdea.name: Redesign before you resign
bigIdea.body: Most people assume the only fix for a frustrating job is a new one. Burnett and Evans argue that you can almost always make your current job work better first, by reframing stuck beliefs, running small experiments and treating “good enough for now” as a base to build on. [1,4,5]

learnings.title: Reframe stuck beliefs
learnings.text: Every chapter starts with a dysfunctional belief and a reframe. Feeling like a cog in a machine becomes being a lever that can move it. [4]

learnings.title: Good enough for now
learnings.text: Not forever, just for now. Accepting that gives you a stable base to improve from, instead of waiting to arrive. [4]

learnings.title: Overwhelm isn't burnout
learnings.text: Overwhelm can be designed around. True burnout or a toxic workplace may be a reason to leave. [5,7]

framework.name: Don't Resign, Redesign
framework.intro: Four options to try, smallest first, before deciding to quit. [7]

parts.name: Reframe and re-enlist
parts.tagline: A new why for the same job
parts.text: Find a fresh reason the work matters to you. [7]
parts.tip: Write down what this job gives you that you'd miss.

parts.name: Remodel
parts.text: Cosmetic or structural changes to what you do. [7]
parts.tip: Trade one task you dread for one you'd enjoy.

parts.name: Relocate
parts.text: Find a different role where you are. [7]
parts.tip: Have coffee with a team you admire.

parts.name: Reinvent
parts.text: Build new skills toward a new career without leaving. [7]
parts.tip: Take on a stretch project.

tools.name: The Good Work Journal
tools.note: This book's version of the Good Time Journal. [4]
steps: Each day, note what you learned, what you initiated, and who you helped.
Keep it going for three to four weeks.
Each week, look for surprises and which category dominates.
Plan one way to grow the missing category.

tools.name: The Maker's Mix
tools.note: Instead of money versus meaning, rate three kinds of making. [3,5]
steps: Score money-making, impact-making and expression-making from 1 to 100.
Set your ideal mix, like faders on a mixing desk.
Close the biggest gap with a small prototype, inside or outside work.
Write your most stuck belief about work, then reframe it.
Score your Maker's Mix.
Choose one of the four redesign options to try.
Start a Good Work Journal tonight.

reflect: If your job were good enough for now, what would you build on first?
Which kind of making is missing from your work?
books.inSedi: Turn your reframe into a project in Timely's Planning view, with the first prototype as its first task.

books.title: The Art of Gathering
books.subtitle: How We Meet and Why It Matters
books.author: Priya Parker
books.pitch: A facilitator shows why so many of our gatherings fall flat, and how to design meetings, dinners, celebrations and even funerals that people actually remember. [1,2]
whyRead: It will change how you host everything, from a meeting to a birthday [2,4]
Memorable stories from gatherings around the world [2]
Specific, surprising advice, like never starting with logistics [2,4]

bigIdea.name: Purpose over category
bigIdea.body: “Dinner party”, “meeting” and “birthday” are formats, not reasons. Parker argues that most gatherings disappoint because we copy the format and skip the purpose. A good purpose is specific, and even disputable: reasonable people could disagree with it. [2,3]

learnings.title: Don't be a chill host
learnings.text: Staying hands-off leaves guests unprotected. Use your authority generously: protect guests, connect them, and treat them as equals. [2,4]

learnings.title: Exclusion is design
learnings.text: Who you leave out, how many people come and where you meet all shape what can happen. [2]

learnings.title: Endings matter
learnings.text: Don't end with logistics or thank-yous. Give a last call, look back at what happened, and help people return to ordinary life. [6]

framework.name: The arc of a gathering
framework.intro: The book follows a gathering from first idea to final goodbye. Five of its moves: [2,4]

parts.name: Decide why
parts.text: Is a funeral to mourn a death or celebrate a life? Each leads to a very different gathering. [2,3]
parts.tip: Ask “why?” until someone could disagree.

parts.name: Close doors
parts.text: The guest list is the first test of your purpose. [2]
parts.tip: Invite only who serves the purpose.

parts.name: Create a temporary world
parts.text: Explicit rules that hold only for this gathering replace unspoken etiquette. [4]
parts.tip: Try no phones, or no job titles.

parts.name: Open with intention
parts.text: Prime guests before they arrive and mark a threshold into the gathering. [2,5]
parts.tip: Send a note that sets the mood.

parts.name: Cause good controversy
parts.text: Invite honesty and productive disagreement instead of everyone's best behavior. [2,4]
parts.tip: As host, go first in being real.

tools.name: 15 Toasts
tools.note: A dinner format described in the book. [4]
steps: Choose a theme connected to the purpose.
During dinner, each guest gives a short, honest toast on it.
Let the evening build, one toast at a time.

tools.name: A closing ritual
tools.note: From the book's chapter on endings. [6]
steps: Give a last call so people know the end is near.
Look inward: one moment to reflect on what happened.
Turn outward: each person names one thing they're taking back with them.
Write its category, then ask “why?” three times.
Rewrite the purpose until someone could disagree with it.
Write two pop-up rules and a 30-second opening.
Design the ending, not just the start.

reflect: What was your last gathering really for?
Who did you invite out of habit rather than purpose?
books.inSedi: Plan the gathering as a project in Timely's Planning view, with its purpose in the event details.

sources.text: Parker, Priya. *The Art of Gathering: How We Meet and Why It Matters*. Riverhead Books, 2018. Ch. 1 Decide Why You're Really Gathering; ch. 2 Close Doors; ch. 3 Don't Be a Chill Host; ch. 4 Create a Temporary Alternative World; ch. 5 Never Start a Funeral with Logistics; ch. 7 Cause Good Controversy; ch. 8 Accept That There Is an End.

University of York, notes on *The Art of Gathering*.
SuperSummary, *The Art of Gathering* summary.

books.title: Our Tribal Future
books.subtitle: How to Channel Our Foundational Human Instincts into a Force for Good
books.author: David R. Samson
books.pitch: An evolutionary anthropologist argues that tribalism is a core human drive we can't switch off, and that we can point it toward belonging and trust instead of division. Winner of the 2023 Balsillie Prize for Public Policy. [1,2,3]
whyRead: A big-picture view of why we form groups at all [4,5]
Practical ideas for building real community [4]
A thought-provoking, sometimes debated argument [6]

bigIdea.name: Belonging is an instinct
bigIdea.body: Samson calls it the Tribe Drive: an evolved urge to belong to groups that helped our ancestors survive. We can't remove it, he argues, but we can choose where it goes, into small, real, trusting groups, or into abstract camps that feed division. [1,4,5]

learnings.title: The trust paradox
learnings.text: Our minds were built for kin and friends, yet we cooperate with millions of strangers. Shared symbols and rituals make that trust possible. [4]

learnings.title: We're under-ritualized
learnings.text: Modern life has lost many of the rituals that once bound groups together. [4]

learnings.title: Beliefs as badges
learnings.text: Samson argues that some beliefs work as signals of loyalty to a group, which is why facts alone rarely change minds. [4,6]

framework.name: The Tribe Drive, redirected
framework.intro: Samson's argument in four steps. Some of his proposals are debated by other scholars. [4,6]

parts.name: The Tribe Drive
parts.text: We evolved to belong to nested groups, from family to band to tribe. [1,6]
parts.tip: Notice which groups you say “we” about.

parts.name: Campcrafting
parts.text: Invest in face-to-face groups like the hunter-gatherer camp of 20 to 30 people. [4,6]
parts.tip: Start with a weekly meal. [4]

parts.name: Ritual
parts.text: Rituals and symbols help strangers trust each other. [4]
parts.tip: Give a group a name or an opening ritual.

parts.name: Metabelief
parts.text: Beliefs that update with evidence, toward a shared identity he calls Team Human. [4,5]
parts.tip: Ask what evidence would change your mind.

tools.name: Map your tribes
tools.note: Inspired by the author's interview on The Hub. [5]
steps: List the groups you're proud to belong to.
Mark each as face-to-face or abstract.
Move time and energy toward the face-to-face ones.

tools.name: Campcraft a circle
tools.note: Applying the book's campcrafting and ritual ideas. [4]
steps: Invite 4 to 10 people to a recurring gathering.
Give it a name or a simple ritual.
Hold it for eight weeks, then decide together whether to continue.
Map your tribes.
Choose one face-to-face group to invest in.
Add one ritual to it.
Practise metabelief: write down a belief and what would change your mind.

reflect: Which of your tribes would show up for you in a hard week?
Where is your instinct to belong being used by someone else's algorithm?
books.inSedi: Put your circle on Timely as a recurring event, and keep ritual ideas in Brainly.

sources.text: Samson, David R. *Our Tribal Future*. St. Martin's Press, 2023. Ch. 1 The Tribe Drive.
Publishers Weekly, *Our Tribal Future* listing.

Krueger, Joachim I. Review of *Our Tribal Future* (2023).

books.title: The Psychology of Interpersonal Relations
books.author: Fritz Heider
books.pitch: A founding text of social psychology. Heider studied the everyday, common-sense theories we all use to explain why other people do what they do. [1,2]
whyRead: The source of ideas you'll meet everywhere in psychology and design [2]
A deep look at how we perceive and judge each other [2]
A classic that rewards slow, careful reading [2]

bigIdea.name: We are all intuitive psychologists
bigIdea.body: We constantly guess at the causes of other people's behavior, and those guesses shape how we treat them. Heider noticed we lean toward explaining others by who they are rather than the situation they're in. Later researchers named that tilt the fundamental attribution error. [2,3]

learnings.title: Naive psychology
learnings.text: Ordinary people have working theories about each other's minds. Heider took those theories seriously as a subject of study. [2]

learnings.title: We see intentions everywhere
learnings.text: In an earlier study with Marianne Simmel, people watching moving shapes described them as having goals and personalities. [2,4]

learnings.title: Relationships seek balance
learnings.text: We prefer our likes and dislikes to fit together, and feel tension when they don't. [2]

framework.name: Attribution and Balance
framework.intro: Two of Heider's ideas still used everywhere from design to diplomacy. [2]

parts.name: Attribution
parts.text: We explain behavior by something inside a person (traits, motives) or outside (circumstances), and over-weight the inside for others. [2,3]
parts.tip: Before judging, list situational reasons.

parts.name: Balance
parts.text: My friend's friend should be my friend. When a relationship triangle is out of balance, we feel pressure to fix it. [2]
parts.tip: Map the triangle to see what's really in tension.

tools.name: The attribution flip
tools.note: Applying Heider's attribution idea. [2,3]
steps: Write your explanation of someone's annoying behavior.
Write three situational explanations.
Act on the most charitable one that's still plausible.
Then ask, don't assume.

tools.name: The balance triangle
tools.note: Applying Heider's balance idea. [2]
steps: Draw a triangle: you, another person, and an issue.
Mark each link + or −.
Find the link causing tension, and decide whether to change a view or accept the difference.
Notice one moment you judge someone's character.
Do the attribution flip.
Draw one balance triangle for a relationship that feels tense.
Have one conversation based on what you find.

reflect: Whose behavior have you been explaining by character rather than circumstance?
Which relationship triangle feels out of balance?
books.inSedi: Write the reflection as a private note in Brainly, and add the conversation as a task in Taskly.

sources.text: Heider, Fritz. *The Psychology of Interpersonal Relations*. John Wiley & Sons, 1958.
Wikipedia, “Fritz Heider”.
Ross, L. (1977). The intuitive psychologist and his shortcomings. In L. Berkowitz (Ed.), *Advances in Experimental Social Psychology* (Vol. 10, pp. 173–220). Academic Press.
Heider, F., & Simmel, M. (1944). An experimental study of apparent behavior. *American Journal of Psychology*, 57(2), 243–259.
